--- title: "Anchored DIF tests for two groups" subtitle: "Item- and threshold-level Wald tests with forward and Gini anchors and a multiplicity correction" author: "Magnus Johansson" date: 2026-11-16 date-modified: 2026-11-16 --- ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false} ## About this chapter **Status:** complete
**Simulated:** Study 1 on 2026-11-13, Studies 2 and 3 on 2026-11-15, with psychotools 0.7-6, multcomp 1.4-30, mvtnorm 1.4-1 and R 4.6.1. Rendered from the cached results with psychotools 0.7.6, multcomp 1.4.30, R 4.6.1.
**Cite as:** Johansson, M. (2026). Anchored DIF tests for two groups. In *Rasch Measurement Explorations*. ::: ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon=false} ## Summary Testing single items for differential item functioning (DIF) requires an anchor that links the two groups' scales. Centring each group on its mean item location, as `RMdifLR()` did up to easyRasch2 1.4.0, flagged items without DIF in up to .870 of datasets when the DIF did not cancel out. Three simulation studies with two groups, 150 to 600 respondents per group, and partial credit or dichotomous items compare the centred scale with the forward anchor of @kopf2015framework and the Gini anchor point of @strobl2021, each followed by a single-step correction over items or thresholds. The forward anchor kept the family-wise error rate (FWER) close to .05 in most conditions and had the most power among the anchors that held it. Its FWER rose to .097 when several items had small location shifts that the selection missed. Its result depends on how tied items are ordered at random, and a consensus over 100 orderings reduced the share of datasets where two runs flag different thresholds from .037 to .012. The Gini anchor point flagged items without DIF less often than the nominal 5%, so some DIF is missed. A test of the spacing between thresholds needs no anchor and kept the FWER at or below .059 in every condition. These results are the basis for `RMdifAnchor()`. ::: ## Purpose {#sec-dif-purpose} Up to version 1.4.0, `RMdifLR()` reported Andersen's likelihood-ratio (LR) test [@andersen1973] together with per-group item and threshold locations, and it flagged items whose largest location difference exceeded a fixed cutoff. The locations were centred within each group, so every item was compared with the mean of all items. When the DIF in a test is unbalanced, the mean item moves too, and items without DIF show an apparent difference. This is the artificial DIF described by @andrich2012. Comparing items between groups requires an anchor. The scale of a Rasch model has no natural origin, so each group's item parameters can only be compared after the two scales have been linked. The LR test compares likelihoods and needs no anchor, but every per-item comparison does. After version 1.4.0, `RMdifLR()` reports only the LR test, and the per-item comparisons moved to the new function `RMdifAnchor()`. The three studies in this chapter are the evidence behind it. Items are compared through an anchor chosen from the data, each comparison gets a Wald test [@glas1995], and the p-values are corrected across items or thresholds. Study 1 (@sec-dif-study1) covers item locations. Study 2 (@sec-dif-study2) covers thresholds, unequal group sizes, and how much the results depend on random tie-breaks in the anchor selection. Study 3 (@sec-dif-study3) checks a consensus anchor over many tie-breaks. The settings studied differ from the defaults of `RMdifAnchor()` in a few places, listed in @sec-dif-defaults. ## Background {#sec-dif-background} ### Anchors {#sec-dif-anchors} The studies compare three anchors. 1. **Centred.** All items, with the locations centred in each group. This is the scale `RMdifLR()` used up to version 1.4.0. It is equivalent to the equal-mean-difficulty method in @wang2004. The all-other anchor gives the same z statistics, since an item's difference from the mean of all items is $(k-1)/k$ times its difference from the mean of the others. 2. **Forward (MTT).** The iterative forward class of @kopf2015framework with the mean test statistic threshold selection of @kopf2015selection. Each item is first tested against several provisional anchors (auxiliary tests), and the items are ranked by how often their test statistic exceeds a threshold based on the mean test statistics. The anchor then grows along this ranking, one item at a time, while it is shorter than the number of items without a significant test against the current anchor [@kopf2015framework]. In `psychotools` the limit is 0.8 times that number, and the top 10% of the ranking are skipped as first candidates. A candidate's own test is not checked before it enters, so an item with a small shift can enter the anchor. 3. **Gini.** The anchor point of @strobl2021. The second group's item parameters are shifted along the scale, and the shift that maximises the Gini index of the absolute item-wise differences is chosen. That is the position where a few items differ a lot and the rest overlap. @strobl2021 [Online Appendix F] show that every optimum of the criterion lies where one item's parameters coincide in the two groups, so the anchor point is always a single anchor item. In psychotools this is `anchor(class = "constant", select = "Gini")`, which by default has length 1. Forward and Gini both assume that most items are free of DIF, and this cannot be tested. When a majority of items share the same DIF, treating them as the reference is an equally valid solution [@strobl2021]. Anchor length is a trade-off. A longer anchor gives more power if it is free of DIF, but a contaminated anchor produces artificial DIF. @teresi2016, summarising @wang2004 and others, report a recommendation of at least four anchor items. The forward anchor grows as long as the data allow. The Gini anchor point is always one item, which @strobl2021 note may cost power. Both are computed with `psychotools::anchortest()` or `psychotools::anchor()`. The first anchor item fixes the scale and is not tested, so $k - 1$ items get a test. When items tie in the ranking, psychotools orders them at random. The forward ranking criterion is a count, so ties are common. The Gini criterion is continuous, and ties are rare. ### Item locations and thresholds {#sec-dif-thresholds} In the partial credit model, threshold $k$ of item $i$ in group $g$ can be written as $$ \delta_{ikg} = \beta_{ig} + \tau_{ikg}, $$ where $\beta_{ig}$ is the item location (the mean of the item's thresholds) and the $\tau_{ikg}$ sum to zero within the item. @henninger2025 distinguish two ways an item can differ between groups. With DIF, every threshold moves by the same amount, so the location moves and the spacing stays the same. With differential step functioning (DSF), the thresholds move by different amounts. Non-symmetric DSF also moves the location. Symmetric DSF leaves the location unchanged and changes only the spacing. Fixing a group's scale adds one constant to every $\delta_{ikg}$ in that group. The constant ends up in $\beta_{ig}$ and leaves the $\tau_{ikg}$ unchanged. Group differences in threshold spacing can therefore be tested without an anchor, and they cannot be affected by artificial DIF. Differences in location, and in the thresholds themselves, need an anchor. ### Multiplicity correction {#sec-dif-correction} Each study tests every item or threshold, so the FWER is the share of datasets where at least one unit without DIF is flagged. The `"fwer"` correction is the single-step max-|z| adjustment [@hothorn2008], which uses the correlation between the tests. Holm's step-down procedure [@holm1979] is reported as a check. @kopf2015framework, @kopf2015selection and @strobl2021 report per-item false alarm rates for dichotomous items. @wang2004 showed for partial credit items, as well as dichotomous ones, that the equal-mean-difficulty and all-other methods fail when DIF is unbalanced. @teresi2016 note that the Kopf et al. results were for binary Rasch items and that they knew of no such evidence for the graded response model. We did not find a study of the forward or Gini anchors for partial credit items, or of anchor selection followed by a multiplicity correction. These are what the present studies add. ## Study 1: item locations {#sec-dif-study1} ### Design {#sec-dif-s1-design} The design has 48 cells with 1000 replications each. Two groups are compared. - **Group size.** 150, 300 or 600 per group, equal in both groups. - **Items.** 10 items with 4 categories (locations evenly spaced on [-1.5, 1.5], thresholds at location - 1, location and location + 1), or 20 dichotomous items (locations evenly spaced on [-1.5, 1.5]). - **Impact.** Group 2's latent mean is 0 or 0.5. The SD is 1 in both groups. - **DIF.** None, one item, three items in the same direction, or two items in opposite directions. DIF is uniform: 0.6 logits added to every threshold of the item in group 2. The DIF items are items 3, 6 and 8 of 10, or 5, 11 and 16 of 20. One DIF item is the first of these, and the balanced pair the first two (+0.6 and -0.6). Each group is fitted by conditional maximum likelihood with `psychotools::pcmodel()`. Replications with a category unused in either group are skipped, since `RMdifLR()` and `RMdifAnchor()` require every category to be used in both groups. Each replication has its own seed. The single-step adjustment is computed with multcomp. The code is in `scripts/dif/dif_wald.R` (methods) and `scripts/dif/dif_wald_sim.R` (simulation). The methods match `psychotools::anchortest()`. With 1000 valid replications, the Monte-Carlo SE of a rate near .05 is about .007, so values from .036 to .064 are consistent with .05. Cells with skipped replications have a wider band, up to .065 with the 840 valid replications of the smallest cell. With many cells, about 2.5% are expected above the band by chance alone. ### Calibration without DIF {#sec-dif-s1-null} ::: {#tbl-dif-s1-null .cell tbl-cap='Study 1, calibration without DIF: SD of z for items without DIF, and FWER with no correction, the single-step correction and Holm. Ranges over group size and impact (6 cells per row). Items: 10 x 4 = 10 items with 4 categories, 20 x 2 = 20 dichotomous items.'} ```{.r .cell-code} nul <- pick(s1, scenario = "No DIF") nul$items <- ifelse(nul$structure == "20 dichotomous items", "20 x 2", "10 x 4") tab <- aggregate(cbind(sd_z_free, fwer_none, fwer_ss, fwer_holm) ~ Anchor + items, data = nul, FUN = function(x) rng(x)) names(tab) <- c("Anchor", "Items", "SD of z", "None", "Single-step", "Holm") kable(tab) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Anchor |Items |SD of z |None |Single-step |Holm | |:-------------|:------|:--------------|:------------|:------------|:------------| |Centred |10 x 4 |.979 to 1.000 |.374 to .403 |.033 to .057 |.032 to .056 | |Forward (MTT) |10 x 4 |1.010 to 1.031 |.411 to .427 |.039 to .068 |.038 to .065 | |Gini |10 x 4 |.840 to .858 |.194 to .206 |.013 to .027 |.008 to .020 | |Centred |20 x 2 |.990 to 1.006 |.608 to .642 |.038 to .058 |.038 to .058 | |Forward (MTT) |20 x 2 |1.003 to 1.019 |.638 to .680 |.049 to .064 |.049 to .060 | |Gini |20 x 2 |.822 to .843 |.304 to .353 |.008 to .017 |.003 to .011 | ::: ::: Without a correction, at least one item is flagged in .411 to .427 of the datasets with 10 items, and .638 to .680 with 20 items, under the forward anchor. The z statistics of the centred and forward anchors have an SD close to 1. The Gini anchor gives z statistics with an SD of .822 to .858. Its tests therefore reject less often than the nominal level, and some DIF may be missed. ### Family-wise error rate with DIF {#sec-dif-s1-fwer} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(s1, aes(n, fwer_ss, colour = Anchor, linetype = Anchor, shape = Anchor)) + annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = 0.036, ymax = 0.064, fill = "grey80", alpha = 0.6) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, colour = "grey40") + geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) + facet_grid(scenario ~ structure + impact_lab, scales = "free_y", labeller = labeller(scenario = label_wrap_gen(18), structure = label_wrap_gen(22))) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(150, 300, 600)) + scale_anchor + labs(x = "Respondents per group", y = "Family-wise error rate") + theme_dense ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Study 1, FWER with the single-step correction: the share of datasets where at least one item without DIF is flagged. The grey band is .036 to .064, the range consistent with .05 at 1000 valid replications. Panel rows have separate y-axes.](dif-anchor-tests_files/figure-html/fig-dif-s1-fwer-1.png){#fig-dif-s1-fwer fig-alt='Grid of line charts, rows for the four DIF scenarios and columns for the two item sets at impact 0 and 0.5, each showing FWER against respondents per group for the centred, forward and Gini anchors. Without DIF and with balanced DIF all three stay near or below .05. With one DIF item and with three DIF items in the same direction, the centred anchor rises above .05 as the sample grows, far above it with 10 items (up to about .87 with three DIF items) and slightly with 20 dichotomous items. The forward anchor stays near .05 and the Gini anchor below it in nearly every panel.'} ::: ::: The centred anchor flags items without DIF as soon as DIF is unbalanced, and more often the larger the sample (@fig-dif-s1-fwer). With three DIF items in the same direction among 10 items (impact 0), the FWER is .239, .470, .870 at 150, 300 and 600 respondents per group. With balanced DIF it holds (.023 to .066). The forward anchor keeps the FWER at .032 to .070 in every cell but one. The exception is .083, with three DIF items in the same direction among 10 items, 150 respondents per group and impact 0. @strobl2021 report a per-item false alarm rate "notably above" the nominal 5% for the forward anchor when 40% of 40 dichotomous items had DIF in one direction, in small and medium samples. Their measure and design differ, but the pattern is consistent. The Gini anchor keeps the FWER well below .05 in most cells (.004 to .027), so some DIF may be missed. It exceeds .05 only in 2 cells, both with three DIF items in the same direction among 10 items and 150 per group (.066 and .071). ### Power {#sec-dif-s1-power} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pw <- s1[s1$scenario != "No DIF", ] ggplot(pw, aes(n, power_ss, colour = Anchor, linetype = Anchor, shape = Anchor)) + geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) + facet_grid(scenario ~ structure + impact_lab, labeller = labeller(scenario = label_wrap_gen(18), structure = label_wrap_gen(22))) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(150, 300, 600)) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) + scale_anchor + labs(x = "Respondents per group", y = "Power") + theme_dense ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Study 1, power with the single-step correction: the mean share of DIF items flagged. The untested first anchor item counts as not flagged.](dif-anchor-tests_files/figure-html/fig-dif-s1-power-1.png){#fig-dif-s1-power fig-alt='Grid of line charts, rows for the three DIF scenarios and columns for the two item sets at impact 0 and 0.5, each showing power against respondents per group for the three anchors. Power rises with sample size for all anchors. The forward anchor is highest with three DIF items in the same direction, close to the centred anchor with one DIF item, and below it with balanced DIF. The Gini anchor is lowest, most clearly in small and medium samples and with 20 dichotomous items.'} ::: ::: Forward has the highest power when DIF is unbalanced (.874 against .725 for centred, three DIF items among 10, 300 per group). It is close to centred with one DIF item, and below it with balanced DIF (.700 against .840, 150 per group). The centred power comes with the inflated error rate shown above whenever DIF is unbalanced. Gini has less power than forward in small and medium samples. With one DIF item among 20 dichotomous items and 300 per group, it finds .263 against .562 for forward. With 10 items and 600 per group the two are close (.986 to .995 for Gini). @strobl2021 also found lower hit rates for the Gini index than for the forward anchor when 20% or 40% of the items had DIF in one direction. With 60% the Gini index had the highest hit rates. In their balanced setting both inequality criteria were outperformed, and they suggest that single-item anchors, which are more affected by sampling error, may play a part. A DIF item was the untested first anchor item in up to .028 of replications per cell for forward and .084 for Gini. ### Run notes {#sec-dif-s1-notes} Replications with an unused category in either group were skipped, up to 16% of them (10 items with 4 categories, 150 per group, impact 0.5). Results there are conditional on all categories being used. One of 48,000 replications failed with an error (‘lower’ not specified or contains NA). When a fit fails, `RMdifAnchor()` stops with a message that names the failing step. The run took 61 minutes on 10 cores. ## Study 2: thresholds, unequal group sizes and tie-breaks {#sec-dif-study2} ### Design {#sec-dif-s2-design} The design has 144 cells with 1000 replications each. - **Group size.** A mean of 150, 300 or 600 per group, either equal or unequal (1.5 n and 0.5 n). Group 2 is the smaller, focal group, with the impact and the DIF. Unequal subgroup sizes and differing latent distributions are among the conditions that make DIF detection harder [@teresi2016]. - **Items.** 10 items with 4 categories as in Study 1, or 20 items with 3 categories (thresholds at location ± 0.75). DIF items are at the same positions as in Study 1. - **Impact.** 0 or 0.5, as in Study 1. - **Scenarios**, as shifts of group 2's thresholds per DIF item: - no DIF - uniform DIF in one or three items (every threshold +0.6) - symmetric DSF in one item (lowest threshold -0.6, highest +0.6, location unchanged) - non-symmetric DSF in one or three items (highest threshold +0.6, location +0.2 with three thresholds and +0.3 with two). Each replication has three families of tests, each with its own correction: 1. **Spacing.** A joint Wald test per item of the group differences in adjacent threshold distances, on $m_i - 1$ df, where $m_i$ is the number of thresholds of item $i$. It needs no anchor. Corrections across items: Holm, Benjamini-Hochberg [BH, @benjamini1995], and a single-step min-p computed from the joint normal of all contrasts. 2. **Anchored thresholds.** Each group is shifted so that the mean location of its anchor items is zero, and $\delta_{ik2} - \delta_{ik1}$ is tested per threshold. Corrections across all thresholds: Holm and single-step max-|z|. 3. **Anchored item locations**, as in Study 1. The prototype reproduces `psychotools::anchortest()` (z identical to within $10^{-14}$). The single-step adjustments are computed by Monte Carlo, with 5000 draws from the joint normal of the estimates. This is the same adjustment as multcomp's, and it is faster with 30 to 40 correlated tests. On one 10-item dataset, with 20,000 draws, the largest difference from multcomp was .003. With 5000 draws, the Monte-Carlo SE of an adjusted p-value near .05 is about .003. In the first 250 replications of each cell (fewer valid ones where replications were skipped), the forward and Gini rankings are redone under 20 seeds and compared with the main run. Only the ranking step draws random numbers, so the auxiliary tests are computed once. The Monte-Carlo adjustments use a fixed seed per replication, so a flag can change only through the anchor. The code is in `scripts/dif/dif_thresh.R` and `scripts/dif/dif_thresh_sim.R`. ### Results {#sec-dif-s2-results} All results use the single-step correction unless stated. Figures show impact 0. Across matched cells, impact 0.5 changed the FWER by at most .027 for the forward and Gini anchors and the spacing test. #### Spacing tests {#sec-dif-s2-spacing} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sp <- sm[sm$family == "spacing" & sm$correction != "none" & sm$impact == 0, ] sp$Correction <- factor(sp$correction, levels = c("ss", "holm", "bh"), labels = c("Single-step", "Holm", "BH")) sp_long <- rbind( data.frame(sp[c("n", "Scenario", "Items", "Sizes", "Correction")], what = "FWER", value = sp$fwer), data.frame(sp[c("n", "Scenario", "Items", "Sizes", "Correction")], what = "Power", value = sp$power)) sp_long <- sp_long[!is.na(sp_long$value), ] sp_long <- sp_long[sp_long$what == "FWER" | sp_long$Scenario == "Symmetric DSF, 1 item", ] sp_long <- aggregate(value ~ n + Items + Sizes + Correction + what, data = sp_long, FUN = mean) sp_long$panel <- interaction(sp_long$Items, sp_long$Sizes, sep = "\n") cor_cols <- c("Single-step" = "#0072B2", "Holm" = "#CC79A7", "BH" = "#D55E00") cor_lty <- c("Single-step" = "solid", "Holm" = "dashed", "BH" = "dotted") cor_shp <- c("Single-step" = 16, "Holm" = 17, "BH" = 4) band <- data.frame(what = "FWER", ymin = 0.036, ymax = 0.064, y = 0.05) ggplot(sp_long, aes(n, value, colour = Correction, linetype = Correction, shape = Correction)) + geom_rect(data = band, aes(xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax), inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "grey80", alpha = 0.6) + geom_hline(data = band, aes(yintercept = y), colour = "grey40") + geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1.8) + facet_grid(what ~ panel, scales = "free_y") + scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(150, 300, 600)) + scale_colour_manual(values = cor_cols) + scale_linetype_manual(values = cor_lty) + scale_shape_manual(values = cor_shp) + labs(x = "Respondents per group (mean)", y = NULL) + theme_dense ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Study 2, spacing tests (no anchor), impact 0. Top: FWER, the share of datasets where at least one item without a spacing difference is flagged, averaged over the six scenarios (items with uniform DIF have unchanged spacing and count as null). The grey band is .036 to .064. Bottom: power to detect the one symmetric DSF item.](dif-anchor-tests_files/figure-html/fig-dif-s2-spacing-1.png){#fig-dif-s2-spacing fig-alt='Two rows of line charts, FWER on top and power below, with columns for the two item sets crossed with equal and unequal group sizes, and one line each for the single-step, Holm and BH corrections. Single-step and Holm stay near or below .05, and BH is higher, up to about .06. Power rises steeply with sample size, is lower with unequal group sizes, and is nearly the same for the three corrections.'} ::: ::: The spacing test needs no anchor, and its error rate does not depend on the DIF scenario (@fig-dif-s2-spacing). The FWER is .011 to .059 with the single-step correction and .009 to .055 with Holm, over all 144 cells. BH controls the false discovery rate, not the FWER. Without DSF it behaves like the others, but with a DSF item in the test its FWER goes up to .092. Power depends on how the thresholds move. One symmetric DSF item is found in .762 to .923 of datasets with 600 per group, and in .530 to .822 with unequal groups of 900 and 300. A non-symmetric shift of one threshold is harder to see in the spacing (.148 to .413 at 600), where only the highest threshold moves and so only the last distance changes. #### Anchored tests: error rate {#sec-dif-s2-fwer} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fw <- ss[ss$family != "spacing" & ss$impact == 0, ] fw$Family <- factor(fw$family, levels = c("locations", "thresholds"), labels = c("Locations", "Thresholds")) fw$panel <- paste0(sub("x", " x ", fw$structure), "\n", fw$ratio, " n") ggplot(fw, aes(n, fwer, colour = Anchor, linetype = Anchor, shape = Anchor)) + annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = 0.036, ymax = 0.064, fill = "grey80", alpha = 0.6) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, colour = "grey40") + geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1.5) + facet_grid(Scenario ~ Family + panel, scales = "free_y", labeller = labeller(Scenario = label_wrap_gen(14))) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(150, 300, 600)) + scale_anchor + labs(x = "Respondents per group (mean)", y = "Family-wise error rate") + theme_dense + theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 7), axis.text = element_text(size = 6), panel.spacing = unit(0.25, "cm")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Study 2, anchored tests, impact 0: FWER with the single-step correction for item locations (left four columns) and thresholds (right four). Columns: 10 x 4 = 10 items with 4 categories, 20 x 3 = 20 items with 3 categories, equal or unequal group sizes. The grey band is .036 to .064 (1000 valid replications). Panel rows have separate y-axes.](dif-anchor-tests_files/figure-html/fig-dif-s2-fwer-1.png){#fig-dif-s2-fwer fig-alt='Grid of line charts, six rows for the scenarios and eight columns for locations and thresholds crossed with item set and group-size ratio, each showing FWER against respondents per group for the three anchors. The centred anchor rises far above .05 with three uniform DIF items, and above it with one uniform DIF item among 10 items and with three non-symmetric DSF items. The forward anchor stays near .05 in most panels and rises to about .1 with three non-symmetric DSF items among 10 items. The Gini anchor stays below .05 almost everywhere.'} ::: ::: The centred scale fails as in Study 1 (@fig-dif-s2-fwer). With three uniform DIF items among 10 (equal groups, impact 0), its FWER for item locations is .199, .482, .863 at 150, 300 and 600 per group, and for thresholds .079, .147, .285. Without DIF, the forward anchor has an FWER of .029 to .074 for locations and .015 to .059 for thresholds. Over all scenarios, 17 of 144 location cells and 4 of 144 threshold cells are above the band for their number of valid replications, against about 3.6 per family expected by chance. The location cells above the band are 3 without DIF, 6 with three uniform DIF items, 2 with one symmetric DSF item, 6 with three non-symmetric DSF items. The largest values are in two kinds of cells. - **Non-symmetric DSF in three items.** Each such item moves its location by only 0.2 or 0.3 logits, which the forward selection often misses. At 600 per group, a DSF item is in the anchor in .333 to .896 of datasets, and the location FWER is .049 to .097. - **Three uniform DIF items with small samples.** With 10 items and 150 per group, a DIF item is in the anchor in .422 to .582 of datasets, and the location FWER is .071 to .077. In both, DIF items enter the anchor. With uniform DIF of 0.6 the selection removes them as n grows (a DIF item is in the anchor in .003 to .014 of datasets at 600 per group), and the inflation goes away. The small location shifts of non-symmetric DSF stay in the anchor more often. With 10 items the inflation then grows with n, because the tests get more precise (.043, .069, .097 at 150, 300 and 600 per group, equal groups). With 20 items it does not (.056, .072, .055). The Gini anchor flags units without DIF less often than the nominal 5%. Without DIF its FWER is .005 to .020 for locations and .012 to .035 for thresholds, and over all scenarios it is above the band in 3 of 144 location cells and 0 of 144 threshold cells (maximum .070). Without DIF, unequal group sizes did not change the calibration. The forward location FWER averaged .052 with equal and .049 with unequal groups. #### Anchored tests: power {#sec-dif-s2-power} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pw2 <- ss[ss$family != "spacing" & ss$impact == 0 & ss$ratio == "equal" & ss$scenario != "null" & !is.na(ss$power), ] pw2$Family <- factor(pw2$family, levels = c("locations", "thresholds"), labels = c("Locations", "Thresholds")) ggplot(pw2, aes(n, power, colour = Anchor, linetype = Anchor, shape = Anchor)) + geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1.8) + facet_grid(Scenario ~ Family + Items, labeller = labeller(Scenario = label_wrap_gen(14))) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(150, 300, 600)) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) + scale_anchor + labs(x = "Respondents per group", y = "Power") + theme_dense ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Study 2, anchored tests, equal group sizes, impact 0: power with the single-step correction, the mean share of DIF units flagged. For locations a unit is an item with a location shift, for thresholds a shifted threshold. Symmetric DSF does not move the location, so it has no location power. For locations, the untested first anchor item counts as not flagged. Every threshold is tested.](dif-anchor-tests_files/figure-html/fig-dif-s2-power-1.png){#fig-dif-s2-power fig-alt='Grid of line charts, rows for the five scenarios with DIF or DSF and columns for locations and thresholds crossed with item set, each showing power against respondents per group for the three anchors. Power rises with sample size. For locations the forward anchor is highest or tied, and the Gini anchor lowest. Threshold power is lower than location power for uniform DIF.'} ::: ::: For item locations the pattern is that of Study 1 (@fig-dif-s2-power). Forward is as powerful as centred with one DIF item and more powerful with three (.883 against .731, 10 items, 300 per group), and Gini has less power than forward (.758 in the same cell, and .831 against .968 with one DIF item). Threshold tests need more data. One threshold shifted by 0.6 is found in .773 of datasets with 10 items and 600 per group under the forward anchor, and in .130 with 150. The threshold test spreads its error rate over 30 or 40 thresholds, so for uniform DIF it is much weaker than the location test (.232 against .968, one DIF item, 300 per group). Unequal sizes cost power. With the same total n, the threshold power of the forward anchor at 600 per group (900 and 300) was 61% to 81% of that with equal groups. #### Dependence on the tie-break {#sec-dif-s2-ties} ::: {#tbl-dif-s2-ties .cell tbl-cap='Study 2, dependence on the random tie-break: ranges over the 144 cells. Over 20 seeds it gives 3.6 to 9.3 different anchor sets per dataset on average, and in .563 to .790 of seeds the untested first anchor item differs from the main run's. Without DIF these differences rarely change a flag (location flags change in .004 to .053 of datasets). With DIF they do. With three uniform DIF items, some seed changes a threshold flag in .071 to .612 of datasets, and the largest value, .612, is at 600 per group (10 items with 4 categories, equal sizes, impact 0.5). The number of true DIF units found also varies by seed, in up to 41% of datasets for locations and 60% for thresholds. Ties are rare for the Gini anchor point. In .000 to .012 of seeds the anchor item differed, and flags changed in at most 1% of datasets. #### Run notes {#sec-dif-s2-notes} Replications with an unused category in either group were skipped, up to 47% of them (10x4, mean 150 per group, unequal sizes, impact 0.5). These are the cells where the smaller group has 75 respondents, and their results are conditional on all categories being used. Six of 144,000 replications failed with an error (infinite or missing values in 'x'). The run took 42 minutes on 10 cores. ## Study 3: a consensus forward anchor {#sec-dif-study3} ### Design {#sec-dif-s3-design} Study 2 showed that the forward anchor depends on the random order of tied items. Study 3 checks whether a consensus over many seeds removes that dependence. For each dataset, the ranking is redone under S seeds, and each item's inclusion frequency is the share of seeds whose anchor contains it. The consensus anchor is the items with an inclusion frequency of at least .5. The auxiliary tests are computed once per dataset, so extra seeds are cheap. Two rules are compared for the untested reference item. In the first, it is the anchor item that is most often first in the per-seed anchors, as psychotools leaves the first anchor item untested. In the second ("all items tested"), every item is tested when the anchor has two or more items. An anchor item's difference from the anchor mean is a well-defined contrast, and the single-step adjustment handles the singular covariance. But the anchor items were chosen because they looked free of DIF in the same data, so their tests lean towards non-rejection, and they add tests to the max-|z| family. The results show the net effect. To measure reproducibility, each dataset is analysed with two disjoint sets of 200 seeds, and the results are compared for S = 1 (the single-seed forward anchor), 50, 100 and 200 seeds within each set. The design is that of Study 2 with impact 0 only (72 cells, 1000 replications each), since impact changed the Study 2 error rates by at most .027. The datasets are the impact-0 datasets of Study 2. As a check, the Gini results of all 144 cell and family combinations agree with Study 2 to within .001 in FWER and .002 in power. The code is in `scripts/dif/dif_consensus.R` and `scripts/dif/dif_consensus_sim.R`, which also source `scripts/dif/dif_thresh.R`. ### Results {#sec-dif-s3-results} ::: {#tbl-dif-s3-calib .cell tbl-cap='Study 3: FWER (mean / maximum over the 72 cells) and mean power with the single-step correction, and the mean number of anchor items. Power is averaged over the cells with DIF in that family.'} ```{.r .cell-code} cal <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(m3, m3$Method), function(d) { lo <- d[d$family == "locations", ] th <- d[d$family == "thresholds", ] data.frame(Method = d$Method[1L], loc_fwer = mx(lo$fwer), thr_fwer = mx(th$fwer), loc_pow = r3(mean(lo$power, na.rm = TRUE)), thr_pow = r3(mean(th$power, na.rm = TRUE)), len = formatC(mean(lo$anchor_len), format = "f", digits = 1)) })) names(cal) <- c("Anchor", "FWER, locations", "FWER, thresholds", "Power, locations", "Power, thresholds", "Anchor items") kable(cal, row.names = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |Anchor |FWER, locations |FWER, thresholds |Power, locations |Power, thresholds |Anchor items | |:--------------------------------|:---------------|:----------------|:----------------|:-----------------|:------------| |Forward, 1 seed |.051 / .089 |.045 / .076 |.440 |.272 |10.5 | |Consensus, 50 seeds |.051 / .086 |.045 / .072 |.442 |.273 |11.1 | |Consensus, 100 seeds |.051 / .085 |.044 / .069 |.442 |.273 |11.0 | |Consensus, 200 seeds |.051 / .088 |.044 / .068 |.442 |.273 |11.0 | |Consensus, 200 seeds, all tested |.048 / .083 |.044 / .068 |.438 |.273 |11.0 | |Gini |.015 / .063 |.021 / .048 |.319 |.189 |1.0 | ::: ::: The consensus anchor behaves like the single-seed forward anchor (@tbl-dif-s3-calib). The error rates and power are almost the same, and the anchor is slightly longer. It does not reduce the contamination seen in Study 2: with three non-symmetric DSF items, the location FWER reaches .088 with 200 seeds, against .089 with one seed. The single-seed values differ from Study 2 on the same datasets only through the tie-break (for example .097 in Study 2 and .084 here, 10 items, equal groups of 600). Testing all items instead of leaving a reference item untested changes the error rates and power by little. ::: {#tbl-dif-s3-agree .cell tbl-cap='Study 3: share of datasets where two disjoint seed sets give a different anchor set or different flags (single-step). Mean over item structures and group-size ratios.](dif-anchor-tests_files/figure-html/fig-dif-s3-agree-1.png){#fig-dif-s3-agree fig-alt='Six small line charts, one per scenario, each showing the share of datasets with different threshold flags against respondents per group, for one seed and for the consensus over 200 seeds. Without DIF both lines are near zero. With DIF or DSF the single-seed line is higher, up to about .15 with three uniform DIF items, and the consensus line stays lower in every panel.'} ::: ::: The consensus reduces the dependence on the seed but does not remove it (@tbl-dif-s3-agree, @fig-dif-s3-agree). Two single seeds flag different thresholds in .037 of datasets on average, and in up to .267 per cell. Two sets of 200 seeds disagree in .011 on average, and in up to .056. Most of the gain comes with the first 50 seeds. The remaining disagreement does not come from too few seeds. It comes from items whose inclusion frequency is close to .5, so that the forward anchor contains them under about half of the possible orderings. With 200 seeds, .072 of all items had an inclusion frequency between .4 and .6, and 44% of datasets had at least one such item. In those datasets the two seed sets gave different flags in .041 of cases, and in the others in .002. More seeds estimate the frequency of such an item more precisely, but it stays near the cut. The most-often-first rule does not give a stable reference item. The two seed sets chose the same one in .475 of datasets, because the first position is spread over several tied items. Testing all items avoids the choice. Replications with an unused category were skipped as in Study 2 (up to 24% per cell). One of 72,000 replications failed with an error. The run took 134 minutes on 10 cores. ## Simulated settings and the defaults of `RMdifAnchor()` {#sec-dif-defaults} The studies were run before `RMdifAnchor()` was written, and its defaults differ from the simulated settings in three places. 1. **Forward anchor.** Studies 1 and 2 used one tie-break ordering per dataset. `RMdifAnchor()` uses the consensus of Study 3, the items in the anchor under at least half of `n_seeds = 100` orderings. 2. **Untested item.** Studies 1 and 2, and the consensus rows of Study 3 except "all tested", leave the first anchor item untested, as `psychotools::anchortest()` does. `RMdifAnchor()` tests every item when the anchor has two or more items. With the Gini anchor point, the single anchor item is untested in both. 3. **Single-step adjustment.** Study 1 used multcomp, and Studies 2 and 3 used 5000 Monte-Carlo draws. `RMdifAnchor()` uses 10,000 draws, so the Monte-Carlo SE of an adjusted p-value near .05 is about .002 instead of .003. The default combination, 100 seeds with every item tested, was not simulated. Study 3 covers each part separately: 100 seeds with the reference item untested, and 200 seeds with every item tested. Their results are close. The location FWER had a mean of .051 and a maximum of .085 with 100 seeds, against .048 and .083 with 200 seeds and every item tested. Two disjoint seed sets flagged different thresholds in .012 and .011 of datasets, and in .011 with 200 seeds and the reference item untested. Above 100 seeds the number of seeds matters little, so the defaults are expected to behave like the "all tested" row. ## Interpretation {#sec-dif-interpretation} 1. The centred scale should not be used to test or flag single items or thresholds. Its error rate depends on whether DIF is balanced, which cannot be known from the data. 2. The spacing test needs no anchor and kept the FWER at or below the Monte-Carlo band around .05 in every scenario, with the single-step correction or Holm. It answers a narrower question, whether the distances between thresholds differ, and it needs large groups to detect one DSF item. 3. The forward (MTT) anchor with the single-step correction kept the FWER close to .05 in most cells and had the highest power among the anchors that held the FWER. Its FWER exceeded the band, up to .097, when several items carried small location shifts that the selection missed, and with three uniform DIF items in small samples. Its results depend on the random tie-break: with the same data, another seed often gives another anchor, and with DIF present it changes which units are flagged in a noticeable share of datasets. A consensus over 50 or more seeds keeps the error rates and power. Two independent seed sets then flag different thresholds in .011 of datasets on average, against .037 for two single seeds (Study 3). The rest comes from items that the forward anchor includes under about half of the orderings, and more seeds do not remove it. Reporting each item's inclusion frequency shows when this is the case. Testing all items avoids an unstable reference item. 4. The Gini anchor point flags units without DIF less often than the nominal 5% (FWER up to .035 without DIF), so some DIF is missed. It has less power than forward in small and medium samples, and is effectively deterministic. Its value remains the criterion plot [@strobl2021]. 5. Threshold-level tests have much lower power than location tests for uniform DIF, because the error rate is spread over all thresholds. Location tests and the spacing test together cover uniform DIF and symmetric DSF. Anchored threshold tests add information mainly for non-symmetric DSF. ## Not covered {#sec-dif-not-covered} More than two groups, DIF sizes other than 0.6, non-uniform DIF in the sense of unequal discrimination (outside the partial credit model), unequal group sizes for dichotomous items, anchors of a length fixed in advance, and anchor rules that would resolve items with an inclusion frequency near .5. ## Revision history {.unnumbered} - 2026-11-16: first version in this book, moved from `easyRasch2/dev/dif_anchor_tests.qmd`.
